8443: The brown-banded bamboo shark (Chiloscyllium punctatum) is one of the most widespread and abundant species of bottom-dwelling sharks in the tropical Indo-Pacific region. This species has potential to provide an important sustainable fisheries resource. However, there is a taxonomic uncertainty issue that may need to be resolved prior to manage its fishery. There is evidence of the variation in body size and size at maturity of the species across the region. An examination of the NADH2 gene region in a study from 2012 also suggests that the Australia’s species is potentially distinct to others. Hence, a comprehensive investigation of this species has been taken using morphological taxonomy and molecular approaches. Here we present the preliminary results based on the morphological assessment to reveal the true identity of this Australia’s species.
8444: The silvertip shark (Carcharhinus albimarginatus) is considered one of the most commonly sighted shark species within reef systems across the Indo-Pacific Ocean. Despite its prevalence, populations are in decline as a result of presumed heavy fishing pressure throughout its range. Knowledge of connectivity and migratory behaviour is essential for effective management. Our study investigated the genetic population connectivity of C. albimarginatus using a mixed-marker approach including - mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) haplotypes at one gene region, 12 newly developed microsatellite loci (Msats) and a panel of 7147 genome wide SNPs developed from double digest restriction site associated DNA sequencing for the same set of individuals. We estimated the dispersal potential and connectivity between regions across the Indo-Pacific Ocean including; Seychelles (n=31), Indonesia (n= 19), Papua New Guinea (n=98) and Australia (n=22). This study is the first to assess the genetic connectivity between populations of silvertip sharks anywhere throughout their range. Results reveal significant subdivision is apparent for populations screened from the Indo-Pacific, with varying levels of differentiation detected by the three marker types. Our findings suggest the following; a. the Indian Ocean is a significant barrier preventing gene flow between the west and central Indo-Pacific, b. broad scale connectivity is present between central Indo-Pacific locations and c. female-mediated site fidelity is likely to be occurring across the Indo-Pacific region. These findings contribute valuable information for the management and conservation of C. albimarginatus.

8445: The biological differences between cartilaginous fishes, even among sharks themselves, are enormous; ecological characteristics, such as life history strategies, respiratory modes, behaviour and habitat use are among the most apparent. Extremes are represented by pelagic, actively swimming, ram ventilating sharks as opposed to bottom dwelling, sedentary species capable of respiring while stationary. Corresponding to these highly variable traits there should be an equally high difference in baseline metabolic rates (MR; measured as O2 consumption). Knowledge of MRs is essential to assess energy allocation to fundamental processes. In the context of fisheries capture stress, determining the MRs of stressed animals will allow estimating the amount of energy that, to cope with stress, has been diverted from these other processes and their resulting impacts. However, data on MRs for different shark species are very scarce, especially for large species. We determined and compared, for the first time, the baseline MRs of two Australian species, Mustelus antarticus and Cephaloscyllium laticeps. M. antarticus is an active, pelagic, ram ventilating species, while C. laticeps is a sedentary, bottom dwelling species able to pump water through its mouth and spiracle. Given the differences in their life strategies, a lower metabolic rate is expected for C. laticeps. Our result showed that, M. antarticus had a higher metabolic rate (186 mg mgO2/h*kg; C. laticeps: 76.26 mgO2/h*kg), additionally it does not seem to recover from the light handling stress imposed. Our results highlight that measurement of MRs are essential to interpret stress responses of species with different ecological characteristics.
8446: Anelasma is a monotypic genus of goose barnacle that uniquely parasitizes deep-sea sharks. Very little is known of Anelasma, as it is infrequently recorded. To date, the genus contains a single species, Anelasma squalicola. This mesoparasite has a presumed widespread distribution, reported from the North Atlantic, Chile, South Africa, and New Zealand. Anelasma has been found on several members of the lanternshark family Etmopteridae, including the Black Dogfish (Centroscyllium fabricii) and the Southern Lanternshark (Etmopterus granulosus), and is thought to impede the development of its host’s reproductive organs. Here, we report Anelasma from a new host family, Pentanchidae, after individuals were found attached to the Roughskin Catshark (Apristurus ampliceps) caught on Chatham Rise, New Zealand. Genetic results indicated the Anelasma specimens were indeed Anelasma squalicola and interestingly, were genetically identical to specimens from the North Atlantic, suggesting this a truly cosmopolitan species. New findings have provided insight into this rarely studied species, and its deep-sea shark hosts.

8447: All chondrichthyans possess ampullae of Lorenzini that allow them to detect weak electrical fields in their surrounding environment. Recent research into this sensory system revealed that the distribution and morphology of these ampullary organs vary from species to species and may be influenced by external factors. This presentation goes over the morphological differences in the electrosensory system of several species of elasmobranchs found on the East coast of Australia and how their ampullary organs are influenced by their diet, lifestyle, and environment. Generally, the ampullary pores of rays are distributed over their heads and pectoral fins, compared to those of sharks that are restricted to their heads and aggregate in different distinctive patterns depending on the species. The ampullary canals of some species possess a peculiar quasi-sinusoidal shape, compared to the usually straight canals, that may be associated with a diet that consists primarily of burrowing infauna. Batoids tend to possess alveolar ampullae which contrasts with the finger shaped ampullae of most galeomorph sharks, but the internal structure remains mostly similar across both superorders, with the exception of the shape of the supportive cells that separate the receptor cells present in each ampulla. More specifically, the supportive cells of rays protrude heavily into the ampullary lumen, a feature never observed in sharks, and the function of which remains unknown.

8448: The eastern coastline is home to an abundant shark population with many shark species, including the White shark (Carcharodon carcharias), Tiger shark (Galeocerdo cuvier) and the endangered Hammerhead shark (Sphyrnidae). The QSCP consists of 344 drumlines and 35 gillnets along the coastline from Cairns to the New South Wales (NSW) border. In recent years, shark populations worldwide have showed signs of large scale declines, especially coastal species such as hammerhead sharks. In this study we aim to infer shark population trends using the QSCP catch data, and to identify peak abundant periods. The QSCP data set was analysed from 1996 due to more accurate species identification by contractors and stable fishing effort. Our results showed a marked decrease in all shark species caught in the QSCP along the study area and overall years. Particularly, the well-known shark species, such as White shark catches have been decreasing to less than one-third, compared to Tiger and Bull sharks that have halved since 1996. White sharks were most abundant in winter, bull sharks are at their lowest during winter, and tiger sharks were present all year. Our results show the endangered hammerhead species (Sphyrnidae) have decreased sharply along the entire Queensland coast. Size analysis of sharks showed the majority of sharks were equal to or less than 2 m in length, indicating juvenile and immature sharks frequent coastal habitats. Further investigation into coastal nursery grounds are needed for Queensland, as hammerheads are listed as globally endangered with projected population declines.

8449: Sharks lack a planktonic larval stage and depend on the active migration of individuals to exchange genes between suitable habitats. The sharks' physical capacity to actively disperse establishes levels of genetic connectivity in the absence of barriers. The ocean, however, is a heterogeneous environment, where the movement of sharks between habitat fragments may be hampered by the presence of physical barriers. The effect of formerly recognised marine phylogeographic barriers on the structure and connectivity of sharks has been discussed on a global scale. Additionally, a range of physical barriers, which can be categorized based on their temporal scale and physical nature, have been found to restrict the dispersal of demersal sharks at various geographical scales. However, studies often lack a strict sampling design, thus limiting the inference that can be made on the effect of these physical barriers. We introduce two case studies with an explicit spatial sampling design to test a priori hypotheses about the barrier effect of ocean depth on the genetic connectivity of shallow-water demersal sharks. Genetic and genomic tools will be used to assess levels of connectivity across depth barriers in whitetip reef sharks (Triaenodon obesus) in the Great Barrier Reef and Coral Sea, and Galapagos bullhead sharks (Heterodontus quoyi) in the Eastern Tropical Pacific.

8450: Shark-diving is part of a rapidly growing industry focused on marine wildlife tourism. Our study aimed to provide an estimate of the economic value of shark-diving tourism across Australia by comprehensively surveying the whale shark (Rhincodon typus), white shark (Carcharodon carcharias), grey nurse shark (Carcharias taurus), and reef shark (mostly Carcharhinus amblyrhynchos and Triaenodon obesus) diving industries using a standardised approach. A socio-economic survey targeted tourist divers between March 2013 and June 2014 and collected information on expenditures related to diving, accommodation, transport, living costs, and other related activities during divers’ trips. A total of 711 tourist surveys were completed across the four industries, with the total annual direct expenditure by shark divers in Australia estimated conservatively at $25.5 M. Additional expenditure provided by the white-shark and whale shark-diving industries totalled $8.1 and $12.5 M for the Port Lincoln and Ningaloo Reef regions respectively. International tourists diving with white sharks also expended another $0.9 M in airfares and other activities while in Australia. These additional revenues show that the economic value of this type of tourism do not flow solely to the industry, but are also spread across the region where it is hosted. This highlights the need to ensure a sustainable dive-tourism industry through adequate management of both shark-diver interactions and biological management of the species on which it is based. Our study also provides standardised estimates which allow for future comparison of the scale of other wildlife tourism industries (not limited to sharks) within or among countries.

8451: The Common Blacktip Shark, Carcharhinus limbatus, and the Australian Blacktip Shark, C. tilstoni are the primary chondrichthyans targeted by the Northern Territory Offshore Net and Line Fishery (ONLF). These sharks are similar in appearance and until recently could only be distinguished through slow and/or destructive means. Despite their similar appearance, these sharks have very different life histories. The Australian endemic, C. tilstoni breeds annually, matures faster and at a smaller size, than C. limbatus, which breeds biennially and is found in tropical and warm coastal waters world-wide. Our aim was to develop a method that would enable accurate field identification of these two species. Ninety seven morphological measurements were collected from 112 sharks (95 C. tilstoni, 17 C. limbatus) identified by precaudal vertebrae counts and genetic analyses. Multivariate and machine learning techniques were used to identify six key measurements (fork length, caudal-fin peduncle height, interdorsal space, second dorsal-fin height, pelvic-fin length and pelvic-fin midpoint first dorsal fin insertion) that can be used to distinguish between the two species. There were also significant differences in pelvic fin markings between species: C. limbatus had a distinct black mark greater than 3% of the total pelvic fin area, while C. tilstoni had either smaller markings, markings with diffuse edges, or no markings at all. The morphological differences identified here will become an important part of a multi-faceted approach to C. tilstoni/C. limbatus identification in the ONLF and will inform the management and conservation of these commercially important sharks.

8452: Visual tuning to the environment is a key adaptation enabling marine organisms to detect prey, mates and predators in the diverse ecosystems in which they primarily occur. Amongst those that experience the most drastic gradients in environmental light conditions are pelagic deep-divers such as mobulid rays (mantas and mobulas). While mobulids forage in epipelagic waters, some species, like the Chilean devilray, are able to dive to 1800 m, likely to obtain deep sea prey. Given extremely conservative life histories and the intense fishing threat that they are presently facing, understanding the biology and ecology of mobulids is essential. Topographic analyses of retinal ganglion cell densities can provide valuable information about the visual ecology of a species by identifying areas of acute vision within their visual field. Our study investigates, for the first time, the visual capabilities of four mobulid species from the Indo-Pacific region, the pygmy devilray (Mobula kuhlii), the Chilean devilray (M. tarapacana), the bentfin devilray (M. thurstoni) and the spinetail devilray (M. mobular). These species have differing lifestyles, ranging from epipelagic to vertically migrating and we therefore expect contrasting retinal specialisations. Retinas show a visual streak across the ventral retinal meridian. This would increase visual sampling of the upper lateral, temporal and nasal parts of the visual field. An area of high cell density is also present in the nasal retina re-enforcing the need for better acuity in the visual field situated behind them. We explore the link between visual specialisations and each species' preferred habitat and behaviour.

8453: The broadnose sevengill shark (Notorynchus cepedianus) is an abundant large marine predator found around coastal New Zealand. Data on the ecology of the species are severely lacking and anthropogenic impacts are unquantified. To partially address this, a study of the demographics of a population at Stewart Island, New Zealand was undertaken. Sampling trips were carried out in each season from winter 2016 to spring 2017. A baited remote stereo-video system (BRUV) was deployed on 81 occasions (mean = 13.5 deployments per season) in a shallow coastal embayment to capture underwater video of the sharks for photo-ID capture-recapture and photogrammetry analysis. Sevengill sharks were recorded on all but one deployment. Extracted images were subject to strict quality criteria, resulting in usable images of 155 individuals that were included in the subsequent analysis. Capture-recapture analysis of these data using Robust Design methods indicated a seasonal trend in abundance ranging from 26 (95% CI = 26 - 30) during winter 2016, to 83 (95% CI 69 - 112) during summer 2017. The observed sex ratio was heavily biased, with females making up 95% of the population in winter 2016 and 73% in summer 2017. Our results pertain to one area only, but are consistent with seasonal trends in abundance seen in other areas with high sevengill shark abundance (e.g. Tasmania). This study presents the first data on abundance of sevengill sharks in New Zealand. These methods will be applied in a wider study with the aim of quantifying the demographics of the species.
8454: The monitoring of commercial shark take in Queensland has traditionally been via logbooks and, at one point, a Fishery Observer Program. Under the Queensland Sustainable Fisheries Strategy, Fisheries Queensland has been developing new monitoring strategies to help understand fishery performance, and ultimately to help ensure the sustainable harvest of sharks. In January 2018, new reporting requirements for both retained and discarded shark catch were introduced. In addition, a monitoring program is being developed to validate the species composition of sharks caught in netting operations in the East Coast Inshore Fin Fish Fishery (ECIFFF) and the Gulf of Carpentaria Inshore Fin Fish Fishery (GOCIFFF). The first objective of this new monitoring program is to determine the species composition of the retained catch. Stratified sampling at ports, seafood processors and at-sea will be employed to representatively sample the retained catch. The second objective is to develop a profile of the discarded shark catch. This will be addressed through multiple angles including a structured questionnaire to document shark discarding behaviour and direct observations of net fisheries with high potential for discarding priority species. This talk will provide an overview of the new monitoring program with the aim of promoting discussion about any challenges, plausible solutions and potential partnerships.

8455: Taylor Maggiacomo is a science illustrator from the United States and graduated with a B.S. in Biology and minor in Art at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, PA. Having recently graduated from California State University Monterey Bay’s Scientific Illustration Certificate Program, she is currently interning at the University of Queensland in St. Lucia creating marine life illustrations in the Tibbetts Lab. Her goal is to make scientific research beautiful and accessible through images that are engaging and educational for a wide variety of audiences. This presentation will outline what science illustration is, why it is important in academia and other educational outlets, and will include some of her work.

8456: Project GenoJaws is a collaborative research project on global shark populations aiming to assess both current and historical populations of tiger (Galeocerdo cuvier), sand tiger (Carcharias taurus), mako (Isurus oxyrinchus) and white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias). Our aim is to estimate population trends through time and space and investigate genetically based adaptation, population connectivity and gene flow. For the project, genetic methods will be applied on historical shark material. Large collections of historical specimens from shark species are found in museums and private trophy collections worldwide and represent a highly valuable source of DNA for retrospective genetic analysis. To overtake the issue of fragmented DNA and possible contamination, typical of historical material, new state-of-art technique will be used. Namely, a sequence capture approach which, combined with appropriate bioinformatics analyses, allow to analyse even very old material. The feasibility of the method have been already tested, and the first results generated for the population of tiger shark along the Australia coasts. The data generated will be used for genetic comparisons over temporal scale for the shark populations object of study, with useful outcomes for informing political and management efforts.

8457: The study of the physiology of Chondrichthyans has been far less investigated than that of teleosts. Indeed, the determination of metabolic rates (MR) has been widely studied in teleosts, but our understanding of this aspect of chondrichthyan biology is limited, which is concerning, given that it is highly relevant for the assessment of the stability of fish population stocks and the management and sustainability of fisheries. So what can be learned from the abundant literature on teleosts? Here we present the methodological challenges and the design solutions we employed on our study of gummy sharks, Mustelus antarticus, and discuss the applicability for other species. In the case of teleosts, the respirometer body is shaped as a cylinder and sealed in the ends which hold inlets, outlets and sensors. While for teleost fish respirometers can be very small, in the case of M. antarticus size was an important constraint in the design of a suitable respirometer. The large, rather stiff pectoral and dorsal fins present another issue, as they are not as flexible as those of teleosts, so the diameter of the respirometer needs to be larger than for a teleost of the same size. Our design allowed us to measure the MR for the first time for M. antarticus. The MR showed a negative relationship with length, and was comparably high, similar to active pelagic species like Prionace glauca. While our data are preliminary, we think that this information can readily be employed by the scientific community.

8459: White sharks (Carcharodon carcharias) have been shown to expand their diet and foraging strategies as they grow. As they approach ~ 3.5 m, they move from consuming inshore teleost and chondrichthyan prey to a mixed diet also including marine mammals and pelagic cephalopods. White shark diet has yet to be investigated in Australia, where ongoing tagging studies have revealed that they rarely travel off the continental shelf. This contrasts the eastern pacific white shark population where large sharks frequently migrate off the continental shelf. We assessed diet using signature fatty acid profiling from 145 individuals ranging from 1.6–5.5 m, collected from Queensland, New South Wales and South Australia. Unlike the ontogenetic diet shifts observed in the eastern Pacific and off the coast of South Africa, white sharks in Australia show no size-related differences in diet or increase in pelagic foraging, with fatty acids (FAs) indicating marine mammal consumption (22:5w3, 20:5w3 or 16:1w7) or pelagic foraging (22:6w3, 16:0, 18:0) remaining similar across all sizes. Furthermore, the levels of these FAs are lower in Australian white sharks than in those from South Africa, indicating that instead of specialized apex predators, the Australian white sharks of all sizes are generalists with comparatively less reliance on pinnipeds as prey items. Revealing this inshore and generalist foraging strategy, suggests the Australian population may be more resilient to changing environmental conditions and specific prey availability.

8463: The reliability of the common methods for shark ageing is increasingly being questioned. Age underestimation is apparent in many studies that count growth bands in vertebrae most likely due cessation of band pair deposition in older animals. Such a process could be combined with underwater behavioral studies conducted through experimental shark feeding in order to aggregate such elusive animals, and then identify and remove ‘problem individuals’. The acurate assessment of the size of the animals through both i) underwater photogrammetry on aggregated animals and ii) thorough forensic analysis of the wounds on humans, would be paramount for profi ling these problem individuals. A detailed morphological study, including the examination of external morphology, dermal denticles, teeth, musculature, neurocranium, visceral arches, pectoral girdle, claspers, and morphometric and meristic data, were performed. Sixteen species are recognized: Scyliorhinus boa, S. cabofriensis, S. canicula, S. capensis, S. cervigoni, S. comoroensis, S. duhamelli, S. garmani, S. haeckelii, S. hesperius, S. meadi, S. retifer, S. stellaris, S. torazame, S. torrei, and S. ugoi. Scyliorhinus duhamelii is resurrected and distinguished from S. canicula by a larger distance between the anterior nasal fl aps (vs. anterior nasal flaps very close to each other), diff used color pattern (vs. color pattern with distinct dark blotches and saddles along the body), absence of cartilage terminal 3 (vs. presence) and a smooth terminal dermal cover (vs. papillose). Scyliorhinus duhamelii presents a more restricted distribution range than S. canicula, with locality records around the Adriatic and Mediterranean Seas. Scyliorhinus tokubee is considered a junior synonym of S. torazame. Information about the distribution ranges of the species was updated, especially for those with wide ranges (S. canicula, S. haeckelii, S. retifer and S. stellaris). Coloration, vertebral counts, maturity size and extension and shape of nasal fl aps are the most useful characters that help distinguish these species. The claspers, underestimated structures in species descriptions, proved to be very reliable for identification purposes with each species presenting a unique combination of characters in their copulatory organs.

Out of the 166 species recorded, only 2.4% are considered to be CR, followed by 3% as EN, 10.2% as VU, 14% as NT, 20.5% as LC, and 39.1% as DD, while 10.2% had no information. The only countries with endangered species lists are Brazil (BAC: 13), Venezuela (13), and Colombia (30). However, despite the lists of somewhat updated species in some countries, there is a great lack of knowledge about their chondrofauna and conservation status in the area, since many species have not yet been evaluated. Data on species distribution, habitat use, nursery areas, and conservation status are scarce and mostly present for a few Carcharhinidae and Dasyatidae species. As a general pattern, most of the catches in the area are obtained through artisanal fisheries. However, several taxa have experienced severe declines throughout the evaluated range, such as Isogomphodon oxyrhynchus, Pristis spp., Carcharhinus spp., Sphyrna spp., Fontitrygon geijskesi, Hypanus gutattus, Styracura schmardae, Gymnura micrura, Diplobatis colombiensis, Narcine bancroftii and Rhinoptera brasiliensis. The greatest threats recognized for the species inhabiting the NCSA are overfishing caused by predatory fisheries, lack of fisheries inspections and data, and key habitat destruction. Furthermore, around 50% of the species in the area lack basic biological information and could be under some level of extinction threat. Therefore, it is a critical conservation region for the Chondrichthyes and urgent conservation action is needed to decrease the effects on their populations.
